claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, non-engineered oxide film.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel initially provides some passivation.
The native oxide film consists of a nonuniform distribution of mixed iron-oxide phases.
FeO is a less-protective oxide component than Fe3O4 in the proposed Q235 system.
Fe3O4 is a comparatively protective and adherent oxide phase in the proposed Q235 system.
At 700–900 °C, aggressive salt penetrates or interacts with the nonuniform native oxide scale.
High-temperature salt exposure accelerates oxide-phase transformation and scale spallation.
An insufficient fraction of protective Fe3O4 causes the oxide scale to lose adherence and expose the underlying steel to rapid oxidation.
A modestly enhanced fraction of stable protective oxide can preserve corrosion protection during high-temperature salt exposure.
Mild annealing may redistribute the native oxide phases or enhance formation of the protective oxide.
Annealing-induced stabilization of the oxide scale would improve Q235 corrosion resistance in aggressive salt at 700–900 °C.
Q235 samples retaining a problematic native oxide will show greater mass change, visible scale degradation, and more surface defects than samples with an annealing-stabilized oxide.
Stainless or alloy steels used as references are known to form protective oxides under comparable exposure conditions.
The proposed oxide-instability mechanism applies specifically to high-temperature exposure involving aggressive salt fluxing.
At room temperature or without aggressive salt fluxing, the native oxide may remain stable enough to passivate Q235 steel.
The proposed study compares as-received Q235 against annealed Q235 under the same salt and temperature exposure while measuring mass change, oxide phases, morphology, defects, and spallation.
Absence of a statistically significant treatment effect on oxide composition, scale stability, and corrosion rate would falsify the proposed oxide-instability mechanism.
